theme: Creation praises its maker; the Spirit renews the face of the ground
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 104:24-35 slowly, twice. Yesterday you read the first half of this psalm. Today you read the conclusion. As you read, notice how the psalm shifts from describing creation to praising the Creator, and how it ends with a startling line about the wicked, before closing in worship.
settingTheScene:
This is the second half of Psalm 104, the great creation hymn we began yesterday. The first half walked us through the order of creation in the same sequence as Genesis 1. Now the psalmist steps back to take in the whole picture, the manifold works of God, the dependence of every creature on his hand, the sea and its creatures, the cycle of breath and death, and finally the worship that all this should produce. The psalm ends as it began: “Bless the LORD, O my soul.”

For new believers, this Psalm is a school of seeing. It teaches us to look at creation not as a backdrop or a resource but as a hymn of God’s craftsmanship.
observation: Verse 24 is the great summary: “O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all.” The whole psalm is gathered into one cry of wonder.
The sea, often a symbol of chaos in the Bible, is here just another part of God’s well-ordered domain. Even Leviathan, the great mythic sea monster, is reduced to a creature who “plays” in the water.
Every living thing is described as dependent on God for food, breath, and life itself. When he opens his hand, they are filled; when he hides his face, they are dismayed.
Verses 29-30 form a remarkable picture: God “takes away their breath” and they die, then “sends forth your Spirit, they are created”, the language of ongoing creation through the Spirit.
The psalmist’s response is to commit himself to lifelong praise: “I will sing to the LORD as long as I live.”
Verse 35 is jarring: “Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more.” Even a creation psalm acknowledges that something is wrong with the world.
The psalm closes with “Praise the LORD”, the first appearance of the word “Hallelujah” in the Psalter.
interpretation:
The second half of Psalm 104 takes everything described in the first half and gathers it into one great act of worship. Verse 24 is the hinge: “O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all; the earth is full of your possessions.” Every creature, every detail, every system in the natural world is the work of God’s wisdom. The psalmist is not just looking at the world; he is reading it as a manuscript of divine craftsmanship.

The sea passage is especially worth pausing over. In the ancient Near East, the sea symbolized chaos, danger, and the realm where gods battled monsters. But Psalm 104 reframes it completely. The sea is just another part of God’s good order. Ships pass through it. Creatures live in it. And Leviathan, the dreaded sea-monster of pagan mythology, is reduced to a creature that “plays” in God’s waters like a dolphin in a tide pool. The God of Psalm 104 has no rivals. What other religions feared, he created and tamed.

Then comes the most theologically rich section: verses 27-30. Every creature looks to God for food. When he gives, they are filled. When he hides his face, they are dismayed. When he takes away their breath, they die. When he sends his Spirit, they are created and the face of the ground is renewed. Christian readers have always noticed the trinitarian echoes here, Father, Spirit, and the implicit Word, at work in ongoing creation. The Spirit who hovered over the waters in Genesis 1:2 is still active in sustaining and renewing what God has made. Creation is not a one-time event in the distant past. It is a present, continuous act of God.

The psalm reaches its climactic resolve in verses 33-34: “I will sing to the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God while I have being. May my meditation be pleasing to him, for I rejoice in the LORD.” The right response to creation is not awe alone, or even gratitude alone, but worship, the deliberate, sustained, lifelong singing of praise to the Creator. This is what creation is for. It is not just a stage on which human dramas unfold. It is a sanctuary in which the Creator is to be worshiped.

And then, just when you expect a peaceful close, comes verse 35. “Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more.” It is a jarring line in such a serene psalm. Why is it here? Because the psalmist cannot praise creation without acknowledging that something is wrong with creation. The world that God called “very good” is now full of sinners and wickedness. Genesis 3 has happened. The psalm refuses to be naive about this. Praise of the Creator and longing for the renewal of creation are not in tension, they belong together. The same God who made all things will one day cleanse all things. And until then, the believer praises him both for what he has made and for what he will yet do.

The psalm closes with “Bless the LORD, O my soul. Praise the LORD.” The first “Hallelujah” in the Psalter. Worship is the final note.
connection: For two days you have been meditating on Psalm 104, God’s creation as ongoing wonder. But notice how the psalm refuses to stop at creation. It ends with a longing for the wicked to be no more, and with an unrestrained burst of praise. This is the same arc you will see throughout this plan: the Bible never stays at creation alone, because creation is broken. The story moves through Fall, redemption, and toward new creation. Psalm 104 already feels the tension and looks forward to the resolution. When you reach Revelation at the end of this plan, the new creation will be the answer to Psalm 104:35, wickedness will be no more, and creation will sing the praise of God forever.
application:
Spend some time today simply praising God for creation. Not as a meditation technique or a stress-relief practice, but as the response that creation itself demands. The psalmist resolved: “I will sing to the LORD as long as I live.” Can you say the same? If not yet, can today be a day to begin?

Practically: walk outside if possible, even briefly, and let yourself see. Notice three things, a tree, the wind, a bird, the warmth of the sun, anything. Name them silently as gifts. Then say, in your own words or in the psalmist’s: “How manifold are your works, O LORD! In wisdom you have made them all.” Worship begins with seeing, and seeing must become saying.

But also, do not flinch from verse 35. The world is broken. There is wickedness in it, in others and in your own heart. Praise of creation that ignores this is dishonest. The Christian’s praise of the Creator always includes a longing for the Creator to come and make all things new. Pray today not just “thank you” but also “come, Lord Jesus.” Both prayers belong in the mouth of every believer who reads Psalm 104.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for the wisdom in what he has made, in your own words.
Thank him for the Spirit who renews, and ask him to renew something in you that feels worn out.
Pray “Come, Lord,” longing for the day when all things are made new.
